title: OutputP versus IncP
formal: Find a natural enumeration problem in \(\mathrm{OutputP}\) but outside \(\mathrm{IncP}\), as requested by Open problem 3.1. The source suggests enumeration of inclusion-minimal dominating sets in graphs excluding a fixed clique as a candidate. It does not define the requirement “natural” or choose a precise lower-bound hypothesis and reduction convention for its accompanying TFNP-hardness suggestion. These choices remain pending; the candidate is not adopted as a replacement target.
why: The direction asks whether the gap between efficient total enumeration and efficient early output occurs in a recognizable mathematical problem rather than only through artificial padding. The known connection to total search makes the hypothesis and hardness standard consequential. A precise completion target is needed before an individual importance assessment or a resolved verdict is justified.
status_note: The 2021/2023 source poses a natural-example direction, not a fully formal yes/no target. The checked 2017 theorem gives an equivalence to TFNP != FP for bare separation, and the 2020 graph theorem supplies only output-polynomial membership of the candidate. Bounded later-work searches through 16 September 2026 did not establish a matching resolution. Because naturalness and the intended lower-bound standard remain unspecified, the card is neither completed nor certified presently open as a precise theorem.
review_note: Source and known-results review completed on 16 September 2026; precise mathematical target remains pending. No artificial separation or proposed candidate was substituted for the source’s natural-example request.

progress.text: Capelli and Strozecki prove that OutputP = IncP is equivalent to polynomial-time solvability of all TFNP search relations; their separation construction uses padding.
Bonamy and coauthors give output-polynomial, polynomial-space enumeration of minimal dominating sets for every fixed forbidden clique size, within a larger graph-class theorem.
The habilitation, deposited on arXiv in 2023, poses the natural-example request and mentions the clique-free domination problem as a candidate rather than an established separation.

sentences: The source asks for a natural enumeration problem with polynomial total time but no incremental polynomial-time algorithm.
OutputP measures the complete output, while IncP also controls the time to produce each initial segment.
Bare separation of these classes is equivalent to the existence of a total polynomially verifiable search problem with no polynomial-time selector.
Minimal dominating sets in graphs excluding a fixed clique have the required total-time upper bound and are suggested only as a candidate.
The naturalness requirement and precise lower-bound criterion remain unspecified, so the card stays pending.

definitions:
The following definitions fix the verified background, without supplying the missing criterion of naturalness. An enumeration problem is a binary relation \(A(x,y)\) on finite bit strings, with the finite solution set \(A(x)=\{y:A(x,y)\}\). It belongs to \(\mathrm{EnumP}\) when membership in the relation is decidable in deterministic polynomial time and a fixed polynomial \(p\) bounds every solution length by \(p(|x|)\). A correct enumeration algorithm lists each solution once, lists nothing else, and terminates. No output ordering is required.

The source uses deterministic random-access machines with a finite program, registers of integers, addition, subtraction and multiplication. Arithmetic is charged according to operand bit lengths; register access and other basic instructions have unit cost. Working space is the sum of the bits held in registers. Solutions are sent to designated output registers. There is no randomization or oracle, and no polynomial space bound is imposed on the two classes here. The source’s convention stops immediately after the final output; equivalently for these class-membership comparisons one can charge polynomially bounded initial and terminal work explicitly. An empty output set must be detected in polynomial input time.

Put \(n=|x|\) and \(N=|A(x)|\). The class \(\mathrm{OutputP}\) consists of problems in EnumP admitting a correct algorithm whose total time, including termination, is at most \(C(n+N+1)^d\), with fixed positive constants \(C,d\). The class \(\mathrm{IncP}\) requires an algorithm and fixed positive integers \(C,a,b\) such that the time from the beginning through the first \(k\) outputs is at most \(C(n+1)^b(k+1)^a\), for every input and every \(1\leq k\leq N\), with a polynomial bound in \(n+N\) for termination. Polynomial preprocessing is included. Constants depend on the relation, never on \(x,k\). The number of outputs and their total encoded length give equivalent polynomial measures because the solutions are distinct and polynomially bounded in length. These definitions give \(\mathrm{IncP}\subseteq\mathrm{OutputP}\).

The search problem \(\mathrm{AnotherSol}_A\) takes \(x\) and an explicitly listed finite set \(S\) of strings, and returns a member of \(A(x)\setminus S\) or a distinguished symbol certifying this difference is empty. Input size counts all bits of the list. Its decision version only asks whether this difference is nonempty. The class TFNP consists of polynomial-time decidable, polynomially balanced relations \(R(x,y)\) with at least one valid \(y\) for every \(x\). Writing TFNP = FP means that every such relation has a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm selecting one valid witness; it does not mean counting or listing all valid witnesses.

For the proposed graph candidate, \(G\) is a finite simple undirected graph on \([n]\), explicitly encoded by its adjacency matrix and vertex count. A set \(D\subseteq[n]\) is dominating if every vertex belongs to \(D\) or has a neighbour in \(D\). It is inclusion-minimal if no proper subset is dominating; it need not have minimum cardinality among all dominating sets. A \(K_t\)-free graph has no set of \(t\) pairwise adjacent vertices. For each fixed positive integer \(t\), the associated enumeration problem lists all its inclusion-minimal dominating sets as distinct \(n\)-bit characteristic vectors. Invalid graphs or graphs violating the restriction can be assigned empty output, since validity is polynomial-time testable for fixed \(t\). In the known output-polynomial theorem, \(t\) is fixed before inputs and the polynomial exponent may depend on it. Although the source algorithm does not require knowing \(t\), its theorem does not assert a common polynomial bound for arbitrary variable \(t\).
answer_criterion: A completion criterion still requires specifying what counts as a natural example and whether the desired lower bound is unconditional or conditional on a named separation, with a definite search-reduction notion if TFNP hardness is required. The original request cannot be certified by omitting naturalness, repeating the known padded construction, or silently replacing it by the proposed graph candidate. Once a precise target is selected, its enumeration guarantee and lower bound would need a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof. No such extra choice is made in this review.

source_formulation.text: Find a natural problem in OutputP but not in IncP; the source suggests TFNP hardness of finding another solution and mentions minimal dominating sets in K_t-free graphs as a possible candidate.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of Open problem 3.1; naturalness and the intended hardness criterion are not formalized by the source.

context_blocks.text: Output-polynomial total time permits a long initial wait when the eventual output is very large. Incremental polynomial time instead limits the cost of producing each initial segment in terms of the input and that segment’s length. The source asks for a naturally occurring problem witnessing this difference, beyond constructions tailored to separate classes.

Capelli and Strozecki prove that OutputP equals IncP exactly when every TFNP search problem has a polynomial-time solution selector. Hence a bare separation is not an unconditional consequence of that theorem: it is equivalent to a major unresolved total-search separation. The shorthand claim of strict containment in the paragraph before Open problem 3.1 must be read with this hypothesis, not as a proved unconditional strictness.

The proof constructs an output-polynomial enumeration problem from any total search relation by attaching many padding strings to every witness. Exhaustive generation becomes polynomial in the enlarged total output, while an incremental algorithm would reveal an original witness quickly. This explains the abstract conditional separation but does not satisfy the source’s further request for a natural problem.

For any problem already in OutputP, completeness of an explicit candidate solution list can be tested in polynomial time in the input and that list. Simulate an output-polynomial algorithm for its time bound at the list size: if it has not terminated, there must be more solutions than listed; if it has terminated, compare all its outputs with the list. The challenge can therefore remain finding another witness despite easy existence testing for another witness.

Bonamy and coauthors prove output-polynomial enumeration and polynomial working space for every fixed forbidden clique size; their main theorem covers a larger graph class excluding a clique disjoint from one edge. This supplies the positive half of the proposed example, but an upper bound on total time does not prove absence of an incremental algorithm. Minimality here is by set inclusion, so the problem does not ask for a smallest dominating set.

The source neither defines an admissible class of natural relations nor chooses a formal reduction behind its TFNP-hardness suggestion. Replacing its goal by arbitrary OutputP/IncP separation, or by the yes/no incremental tractability of a fixed-clique domination problem, would change the requested result. Those are concrete possible reformulations, not consequences of merely unpacking the existing wording.

statement_review.remaining_issue: Open problem 3.1 requires a natural example but gives no mathematical naturalness criterion; its TFNP-hardness suggestion does not fix reductions or a precise conditional lower-bound target. The abstract padded separation is already equivalent to TFNP != FP, and the K_t-free dominating-set problem is only a candidate. Completing the card requires an explicit choice among these materially different goals.
